mcqs.question: Run-length encoding "c" (a run of length 1, no repeats) — how should it be written according to the standard rule?
options: "c1" — every run gets an explicit count, including runs of length 1
"c" — single characters are left unencoded
"1c" — the count is written before the character
It's omitted entirely from the output since it isn't a real run
mcqs.explanation: The rule writes character-then-count for every run with no special case for singles, so a run of 1 becomes "c1", not the bare character. This is also why single-character runs make the encoded output longer, not shorter — an important trade-off covered later.

mcqs.question: In the in-place compression implementation, why does the read cursor fully count a run before the write cursor writes anything for it?
options: Because writing must always happen before reading in an in-place algorithm
Because the write cursor needs the complete count before it can write the character-plus-count output for that run
It's an arbitrary ordering choice with no effect on correctness
Because Python requires reads to precede writes within the same loop
mcqs.explanation: The run's count isn't known until the read cursor has scanned past every repeated character in it, so the write can't commit the character-plus-count output any earlier without guessing. The ordering is required for correctness, not arbitrary or language-specific.

mcqs.question: A run of 11 identical characters needs to be encoded. What's the risk if the code assumes the count always fits in one output slot?
options: There is no risk — counts are always single digits by definition
The algorithm crashes immediately with an index error
The count "11" gets truncated or malformed, since it needs two character slots, not one
The run gets skipped entirely and produces no output
mcqs.explanation: A run of 11 has a two-digit count, and assuming a single output slot is exactly the bug — the fix is writing each digit of the count separately, since counts of 10 or more genuinely need multiple slots. This doesn't produce a clean crash or a dropped run; it silently malforms the output.

mcqs.question: What invariant must an in-place compression algorithm maintain to avoid corrupting unread data?
options: The write cursor must always move exactly twice as fast as the read cursor
The read cursor must process the string in reverse order
The write cursor must only write at even-numbered indices
The write cursor must never advance past the read cursor's current position
mcqs.explanation: The required invariant is that write never exceeds read, since writing past that point overwrites characters the read cursor hasn't examined yet. There's no fixed speed ratio, no requirement to process in reverse, and no even-index restriction involved.

mcqs.question: For which run lengths does run-length encoding actually produce a shorter result than the original run?
options: Runs of length 3 or more — length-1 runs get longer, length-2 runs stay the same size
Only runs of length exactly 2
Every run length, including 1 and 2
Only runs whose length is a multiple of 10
mcqs.explanation: A run of 1 encodes to 2 characters (longer), a run of 2 encodes to 2 characters (same size), and only runs of 3 or more actually shrink — which is why the interview version of this problem checks whether the compressed result is actually shorter before using it. Runs of length 2 don't shrink, and length isn't restricted to multiples of 10.

mcqs.question: Decoding the compressed string "a11b2", what count should be read for the first character?
options: 1, stopping at the first digit character encountered
It's ambiguous and cannot be decoded correctly
11, since the digit-reading loop continues consuming digit characters until a non-digit appears
111, treating every digit including the '2' from the next pair as part of the first count
mcqs.explanation: A correct decoder reads digits in a loop until hitting a non-digit character, so "11" is read as the full count for 'a', not just its first digit. It isn't ambiguous as long as digit-reading continues properly, and it must stop before consuming the next character-count pair's digits.
